paragraphs: No man has natural authority over his fellow, and force creates no right. We must conclude, then, that conventions are the basis of all legitimate authority among men.

If an individual can give away his liberty and make himself the slave of a master, says Grotius, why could a whole people not do the same and make itself subject to a king? This passage contains plenty of ambiguous words that would need explaining, but let us stick to the word _alienate_. To alienate is to give or to sell. Now a man who becomes another’s slave does not give himself; he sells himself, at the very least for his subsistence. But what does a people sell itself for? Far from supplying his subjects with their subsistence, a king gets his own only from them, and, as Rabelais says, kings do not live on nothing. Do subjects, then, give their persons on condition that the king takes their property as well? I fail to see what they have left to keep.

It will be said that the despot guarantees his subjects civil peace. Granted. But what do they gain from it if the wars his ambition brings down on them, his insatiable greed and the harassment of his ministers hurt them more than their own quarrels would have? What do they gain if the very peace they enjoy is one of their miseries? There is peace in dungeons too, but does that make dungeons good places to live? The Greeks shut up in the Cyclops’ cave lived there quite peacefully while they waited their turn to be eaten.

To say that a man gives himself for nothing is to say something absurd and unthinkable. Such an act is void and illegitimate for the simple reason that whoever does it is out of his mind. To say the same of a whole people is to imagine a people of madmen, and madness creates no right.

Even if each man could give himself away, he could not give away his children. They are born men and free. Their liberty belongs to them, and no one but them has the right to dispose of it. Before they reach the age of reason, their father may, in their name, set conditions for their survival and well-being, but he cannot give them away irrevocably and unconditionally. Such a gift goes against the purposes of nature and exceeds a father’s rights. So to make an arbitrary government legitimate, the people in every generation would have to be free to accept or reject it. But if that were so, the government would no longer be arbitrary.

To renounce liberty is to renounce being a man, to give up the rights of humanity and even its duties. No compensation is possible for someone who gives up everything. Such a renunciation cannot be reconciled with man’s nature: to take all liberty from his will is to take all morality from his acts. Finally, a convention that sets up absolute authority on one side and unlimited obedience on the other is empty and self-contradictory. Is it not clear that we can have no obligation to a person from whom we have the right to demand everything? Does this condition alone, with no equivalence or exchange, not make the act void? For what right can my slave have against me, when everything he has belongs to me? His right being mine, a right of mine against myself is a phrase with no meaning.

Grotius and the others find another origin for the so-called right of slavery in war. They hold that the victor has the right to kill the vanquished, so the vanquished can buy back his life at the price of his liberty, and this convention is all the more legitimate because it benefits both parties.

But it is clear that this supposed right to kill the conquered cannot be derived from the state of war in any way. While men live in their original independence, their relations are not stable enough to constitute either a state of peace or a state of war, and for that reason alone they cannot be natural enemies. War is constituted by a relation between things, not between persons. And since the state of war cannot arise from mere personal relations, only from real relations, private war, or war of man against man, can exist neither in the state of nature, where there is no settled property, nor in the social state, where everything is under the authority of the laws.

Individual combats, duels and encounters are acts that cannot constitute a state. As for the private wars that the Establishments of Louis IX, King of France, authorized and the Peace of God suspended, they are abuses of feudalism, which is in itself as absurd a system as ever existed, and contrary to the principles of natural right and to all sound political order.

War, then, is not a relation between one man and another but between one State and another. Individuals are enemies only by accident: not as men, nor even as citizens,[1] but as soldiers; not as members of their country but as its defenders. Finally, each State can have only other States as enemies, not men, since there can be no real relation between things of different natures.

This principle also agrees with the established rules of every age and the constant practice of all civilized peoples. A declaration of war is a notice given less to the powers than to their subjects. A foreigner, whether king, individual or people, who robs, kills or detains subjects without having declared war on the prince is not an enemy but a brigand. Even in real war, a just prince seizes everything in the enemy’s country that belongs to the public, but respects the lives and goods of individuals; he respects the rights on which his own are founded. The aim of the war is to destroy the hostile State, so the other side has the right to kill its defenders for as long as they bear arms. But as soon as they lay them down and surrender, they cease to be enemies or instruments of the enemy and become simply men again, and no one has any right to take their lives. Sometimes it is possible to kill the State without killing a single one of its members; and war gives no right that is not necessary to achieving its aim. These principles are not those of Grotius. They do not rest on the authority of poets; they are derived from the nature of reality and founded on reason.

The right of conquest has no basis other than the right of the strongest. If war does not give the conqueror the right to massacre conquered peoples, the right to enslave them cannot rest on a right that does not exist. No one has a right to kill an enemy except when he cannot make him a slave, so the right to enslave him cannot be derived from the right to kill him. It is therefore an unfair exchange to make him buy his life, over which the victor holds no right, at the price of his liberty. Is it not clear that it is a vicious circle to found the right of life and death on the right of slavery, and the right of slavery on the right of life and death?

Even if we grant this terrible right to kill everybody, I maintain that a slave made in war, or a conquered people, owes its master nothing except obedience, and only as far as it is forced to obey. By accepting an equivalent for his life, the victor has done him no favor: instead of killing him pointlessly, he has killed him usefully. So far is he from gaining any authority over him beyond that of force that the state of war continues between them. Their relation is itself the effect of it, and exercising the right of war does not imply a treaty of peace. A convention has indeed been made, but far from ending the state of war, it presupposes that it continues.
